title: Elderberry syrup
subtitle: The classic winter immune-support syrup
excerpt: Five hundred grams of dried elderberries simmered in one litre of water until reduced by half, strained, cooled, and stirred into an equal volume of honey. Traditionally taken through winter as a general immune-support tonic. Makes approximately 500 ml, which keeps refrigerated for six months.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), Elder (Sambucus nigra) entry : elderberry preparations and syrups. King's American Dispensatory (Felter and Lloyd, 1898), Sambucus section. EMA HMPC monograph considerations on Sambucus nigra : safety note on raw berry glycoside content.

recipe.yieldDescription: Approx 500 ml syrup (about 100 preventive doses or 25 acute doses)
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Store refrigerated in a sealed glass bottle. Keeps for 6 months. Prepare annually at the start of autumn.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Refrigerate in a sealed glass bottle. Use within 6 months. Discard if it smells fermented, the colour changes significantly, or any mould appears.

glossaryTerms.definition: A preserved liquid preparation made by combining a strained decoction or strong infusion with honey or sugar to extend shelf life and improve palatability.

content.text: Elderberry syrup is a dark, sweet

made by simmering dried Sambucus nigra berries in water until the liquid reduces by half, then straining and combining with honey. Cooking is essential: raw elderberries contain cyanogenic glycosides that cause nausea and vomiting. Cooking breaks these down and makes the syrup safe. Traditionally taken through the winter months as a general immune-support tonic, and at higher doses at the first sign of a cold. Makes approximately 500 ml, enough for a full winter season of daily use.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body:
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Do not eat or prepare raw elderberries. Raw berries contain cyanogenic glycosides that cause nausea and vomiting. This syrup is safe because the berries are cooked; the heat breaks down the glycosides. Always cook elderberries before use.

Readers with autoimmune conditions (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, and similar) should consult a herbalist before taking elderberry syrup long-term, as it modulates immune activity.

Paediatric use is not adult-divided-by-half. Consult a herbalist who specialises in children's herbal medicine before giving elderberry syrup to children under twelve. Honey-containing preparations should not be given to infants under 12 months (risk of infant botulism).

content.text: Place 500 g of dried elderberries and one litre of cold water in a medium saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer.
Simmer uncovered for 35-45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the liquid has reduced by roughly half. The berries should be soft and the liquid deep purple-red.
Remove from the heat and leave to cool for 10 minutes. Strain through muslin cloth into a measuring jug, pressing the spent berries to extract all the liquid. Discard the spent herb.
Leave the strained liquid to cool to below 40°C before adding the honey. Adding honey to hot liquid destroys its active compounds. Stir in 500 ml of honey until fully combined.
Pour into a sterilised glass bottle or jar with a tight-fitting lid. Seal, label with the date, and refrigerate.

Preventive dose: 1 teaspoon once a day throughout the cold and flu season (fall through early spring). Acute dose: 1 teaspoon four times a day at the first sign of a cold or flu, for up to seven days. If symptoms persist beyond seven days or worsen, stop and see your doctor.

Refrigerate in a sealed glass bottle. The syrup keeps for six months refrigerated. Discard if it smells fermented, the colour changes significantly, or any mould appears. Always use a clean spoon to avoid contaminating the bottle.
When not to use this remedy
Do not give this syrup to infants under 12 months (honey content, infant botulism risk).
See a doctor if symptoms last more than ten days, fever rises above 39°C, breathing is laboured, or symptoms worsen after at first improving.
